L-0001.note: Opening line of the note: this session is all about distributed ID generators. The garbled 'third day second' is not quoted; the course order gives week 3, day 2.

L-0002.note: 'One of the most misunderstood topics'; the garbled clause is read, hedged, as 'people assume auto-increment is enough'.

L-0003.note: Most teams meet the problem only at scale, and reach that scale sooner than they think.

L-0004.note: Reason 2: the computer science behind the solutions is beautiful (one clause, no hype).

L-0005.note: Reason 3: side effects most people never think about; forward link to section 8.

L-0006.note: The plan: foundations first, then Amazon, Flickr, Twitter, Instagram, plus one side effect worth a demo (named as pagination in L-0100).

L-0007.note: 'How to use this page': implement every approach; past cohorts understood far more. Echoed in the 9.2 'Build them all' margin note.

L-0008.note: Definition of an ID: anything that uniquely identifies a row, document, object or event.

L-0009.note: Problem statement in one sentence: a function that returns something unique every time it is called.

L-0010.note: RuleBox §1: start with a function in your business logic, invoked locally per request; a central service only later if needed.

L-0011.note: v1: return the current epoch millisecond, because time is unique and moves forward. Board code shown.

L-0012.note: 'Something must break, or everyone would use it': the hook into 2.2.

L-0013.note: Millisecond granularity: two calls in one ms collide unless you go finer. Fig 2.a (D-01) carries the board line 'works on one machine if never called twice in one ms'.

L-0014.note: Two machines, same ms, both 1729: collision. Fig 2.b panel 1 (D-02) with both t = 1729 ringed red.

L-0015.note: Fix: concatenate the machine ID, m1-1729 / m2-1729 (naming is arbitrary). Fig 2.b panel 1 label line; CodeBlock concat(machine_id, get_epoch_ms()).

L-0016.note: RuleBox §2: whenever you see a collision, add the thing that led to it. Echoed on the 9.2 heuristics card.

L-0017.note: Threads on several cores collide inside one machine: m1-1729 twice.

L-0018.note: Aside, one clause: thread IDs are OS-assigned integers; T1/T2 is shorthand.

L-0019.note: Fix 1 for threads: m1-t1-1729. Fig 2.b panel 2 (D-03); the board's 'm2-t3' slip is drawn as m2-t2.

L-0020.note: Fix 2 for threads: add a counter (commonly one that resets every few minutes).

L-0021.note: Why: always appending the cause makes gigantic IDs; a counter avoids that.

L-0022.note: Static counter defined: one process-wide variable all threads share, incremented atomically. Light inline clarification (imprecise/low): static storage, not the heap.

L-0023.note: getid() = machine + ts + counter++: m1-1729-01/02/03, then m1-1730-... Fig 2.c step 2 (D-04 first form; board slip 'm3' drawn as m2). CodeBlock with the counter.

L-0024.note: The increment must be atomic: lock/mutex or a native atomic. Link back to Lecture 2's count++ race.

L-0025.note: When to reset is business logic; uniqueness holds because the ms moves on, as long as the counter stays under the integer limit.

L-0026.note: Summary sentence: two ways to beat thread collisions (thread ID, or atomic counter for any number of threads).

L-0027.note: The sharp move: with an atomic counter, time is redundant; drop it, ID = machine + counter (m101, m102). Fig 2.c steps 3-4 (D-04 final form, time struck out).

L-0028.note: Limit: the counter can hit the integer limit (~4 billion); 2^64 you'll never hit. Simplified/low: left as taught ('~4 billion' is the unsigned 32-bit figure, correct as such).

L-0029.note: Machine ID + atomic counter solves uniqueness (closing line of 2.3).

L-0030.note: Reboot resets the in-memory counter to 0; the machine reissues m101, m102.

L-0032.note: Class idea: back the counter up to a local file; accepted because volatility is the problem. 'One idea raised in class'.

L-0033.note: File-backed counter: load() at start, counter++ then save on every call. Simplified/low, left as taught; A-IG-03 woven in as a separate sourced sentence (fsync, page cache). Board label 'Fault Tolerance'.

L-0034.note: Loading once at boot is fine.

L-0035.note: Problem 1 of saving every call: a disk IO per ID, many micro IOs, heavy disk pressure.

L-0036.note: Problem 2: latency, disk IO every time instead of memory.

L-0037.note: Class idea (a): boot counter as a third ID part, written once per startup; in-memory counter never saved per call. Revealed in P2 and stated in prose.

L-0038.note: Boot-counter costs: the startup increment must be atomic; the ID gets longer.

L-0039.note: It tackles disk IO head on; the long-ID cost is picked up in section 4 (link to 4.5 L-0149).

L-0040.note: Class idea (b): bank of IDs, read 1, store 1001, serve 1000 from memory. Revealed in P2 and in prose.

L-0041.note: Reframed as periodic writes; 'comes in handy at two different places' with links to 2.6 and 5.2.

L-0042.note: Flush frequency: write every N (e.g. 1000) IDs, 1000x fewer disk IOs.

L-0043.note: Code: counter = load() + N; counter++; if counter % N == 0 then save. Board code.

L-0044.note: Worked example N = 3: flush 3 and 6, issue 7 and 8, crash; restarting at 6 reissues 7 and 8. Fig 2.d (D-05) steps 1-4; also the clip l03-flush-crash and P3.

L-0045.note: Safest value = last flushed + N + 1 = 6 + 3 + 1 = 10 (m1-10). Note that load() + N = 9 and the first ++ gives 10, so code and board agree. Fig 2.d step 5; clip; P3 reveal.

L-0046.note: 8 and 9 never used: fine, correctness over using every integer. Also in the clip's last caption.

L-0047.note: Takeaway 1: periodicity via a mod, not a timer thread.

L-0048.note: Takeaway 2: on recovery start from the safest value; think correctness. Reused in 5.8 (L-0186) and on the 9.2 heuristics card.

L-0049.note: Opening problem of section 3: machine + counter IDs carry no order; m1 can be anything.

L-0050.note: New constraint: globally increasing IDs wherever the request lands.

L-0051.note: Why: Lecture 3's airline check-in, T1 and T2 ordered by number. ForwardChip-style back-link to Lecture 3.

L-0052.note: Newer write wins: the larger number marks the newer write. Fig 3.a (D-06: a = 10, T1 -> 20, T2 -> 30).

L-0053.note: Hedge kept: one of the places, not all, where ordered IDs matter.

L-0054.note: Monotonic vs strictly monotonic, as taught (1 2 3 4 5 6 vs 1 2 5 7 8 9 32 33 34). Light inline clarification (imprecise/low): increasing with gaps allowed; gap-free is usually called sequential.

L-0055.note: Flip to time-then-machine; time in the most significant digits sorts IDs. Fig 3.b (D-07 sorted column).

L-0056.note: The lower part can be machine or counter; Fig 3.b annotation 'conflict in the first half, tie break in the second'.

L-0057.note: Within one ms the order can flip (17290002 before 17290001); across ms almost monotonic.

L-0058.note: Still stateless, no central state, excellent throughput; accepts a little incorrectness.

L-0059.note: Aside: with an integer machine ID the whole ID is just bits (sets up section 6).

L-0060.note: 'Time on the leftmost side' of every ID generator. Light inline (imprecise/low): IDs sort roughly by creation time. On the 9.2 heuristics card.

L-0061.note: Good but not a guarantee; the within-ms flip is one reason (board: clocks out of sync, leads into 3.4).

L-0062.note: The design assumed synchronized clocks; they aren't.

L-0063.note: Within-ms misordering tolerable, second-level not; that's where clocks bite.

L-0064.note: SRE/DevOps teams sync clocks to NTP. Simplified/low: left as taught; the daemon nuance lives in the 3.4 margin note 'How clocks are actually synced' as its own topic (with A-IG-02), not as a correction.

L-0065.note: Why clocks drift: a quartz crystal's vibrations are counted.

L-0066.note: Physics analogy (energy -> vibration; boiling, freezing), one sentence.

L-0067.note: Heat runs the clock fast, cold slow. SourceNote SN-01 right after (wrong/low): both extremes slow a common crystal (parabolic curve), A-IG-25.

L-0068.note: Physics nudges clocks, so sync runs more often than you think.

L-0069.note: 'You can't run away from nature': Jeff Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat chasing a flipped bit. Unverifiable: attributed to the lecture; article named by its real title, The New Yorker, 'The Friendship That Made Google Huge'.

L-0070.note: Even with periodic sync, a clock can be off at the moment an ID is made. Fig 3.c.

L-0071.note: Machines 2,4,7,9 at 23,24,23,23; requests in order give 232, 244, 237, 239 (arithmetic checked). Fig 3.d (D-08); clip l03-clock-skew; P4.

L-0072.note: Where order is needed, skew affects correctness and must be handled.

L-0073.note: 'Almost impossible' (hedge kept; no proof, many practical breakers). Simplified/low: left as taught; the 'you pay with coordination' footnote is A-IG-20/21 in 3.7.

L-0074.note: Central ID service: one machine, a network call per ID. Fig 3.e (D-09).

L-0075.note: At this point the problem becomes clock synchronization, not ID generation (board line).

L-0076.note: 'The clock never goes back in time. Never.' kept as taught, then SourceNote SN-02 (wrong/high): small offsets are slewed, larger ones can step back; generators must detect it. A-IG-01, A-IG-02.

L-0077.note: One server gives increasing IDs; SourceNote SN-03 (imprecise/medium): only if it guards against a backward step (Snowflake waits; or a monotonic clock).

L-0078.note: SPOF -> a second machine behind a load balancer (link to Lecture 5). Board nuance: the server or its disk can fail.

L-0079.note: Two ID servers must ask each other for the last ID, add a buffer, then answer. Fig 3.f (D-10).

L-0080.note: Constant gossip makes it complex and slow; board 'we made the entire process super complicated'. Fig 3.f gossip arc scribbled red.

L-0081.note: No distributed service with strict monotonicity at high throughput. Light inline (imprecise/low, overridden): systems that do it pay with coordination (TiDB's one allocator, Spanner's clock hardware), A-IG-20, A-IG-21. Part of RuleBox §3.

L-0082.note: Every fix brings a new problem, so people relax constraints; board 'non-integer IDs, no monotonicity'.

L-0083.note: Objection 'MySQL has monotonic IDs': one machine, the engine owns the counter. Simplified/low, left as taught; A-IG-13 woven in (gaps after rollback are normal). Previewed in 1.2.

L-0084.note: Multi-master MySQL with auto-increment would conflict. Simplified/low, left as taught; A-IG-12 woven in (Group Replication sets increment/offset: uniqueness, not order).

L-0085.note: Everything is a trade-off. On the 9.2 heuristics card.

L-0086.note: Ask whether you need each constraint (integers? random? monotonic?); requirements often weren't thought through. RuleBox §3 body.

L-0087.note: The opening problem: two masters both auto-increment 1, 2, 3, 4 and collide. Fig 1.a redraws D-11 with the colliding IDs ringed red.

L-0088.note: So you can't rely on database IDs and need your own ID logic (e.g. machine ID); forward links to sections 5-7.

L-0089.note: Q&A folded: a shared database with locks is unique but is the same thing, a shared service on one machine.
